title: NASA Rover Discovers Preserved Organic Carbon in Rocks from an Ancient Martian River, Renewing Search for Extraterrestrial Life
excerpt: NASA's Perseverance rover discovers organic carbon in ancient Martian rocks, renewing the quest for signs of extraterrestrial life.
content:
Study Published in Science Advances Reveals the Presence of Carbon Molecules in Samples Collected by the Perseverance Rover, Reinforcing Research on Habitable Environments on the Red Planet.

A new study has revealed the discovery of organic carbon compounds in rocks from an ancient river system on Mars. The analysis provides new clues regarding the planet’s ability to preserve traces of past life.

Discovery of Organic Carbon in Jezero Crater

The research was based on data collected by NASA’s Perseverance rover, which explores Jezero Crater. The area once housed a lake fed by rivers that may have transported and deposited chemical compounds over time.

The analyzed samples date back to a period when the planet had a more active water cycle. The preservation of these chemical structures allows for investigation of environmental conditions from billions of years ago.

Origin of Molecules and Geological Processes

Scientists emphasize that the detection of organic carbon does not prove the existence of biological activity in the area. Similar structures may arise from non-biological processes, such as volcanic reactions, interactions between water and minerals, or impacts from space objects.

The structure and composition of the compounds are still under analysis to determine their exact origin. The stability of Martian rocks provides a preserved record, unlike Earth, where plate tectonics and erosion alter the surface.

Comparisons with Ancient Earth Records

On Earth, complex macromolecular compounds serve as fundamental building blocks for life and are found in ancient rocks. They often represent the only remaining organic evidence of past microorganisms.

Researcher Ashley Murphy from the Planetary Science Institute and co-author of the study stated to Space.com that carbon is the primary building block of terrestrial life. According to the scientist, since primitive Mars may have been similar to Earth, the goal is to understand if the planet ever had the conditions and ingredients necessary to support life.
